I am not interested in that point. I cannot conceive of such a conciliation body being in a position to give a fair judgment. They may be able to decide which party is guilty and which party is innocent, but surely the board which hears the evidence and pronounces upon the guilt or innocence of the parties is the logical authority to impose the penalty. But that is not the set-up. When the board gets the evidence it is turned over to a magistrate who imposes the penalty.
I am not going to review the whole bill, but at this point I want to turn to the last two subsections. Subsection (5) provides:
If, in the opinion of a magistrate, the order of the board is ambiguous or its meaning not clear in any particular, he may refer to the board any question or matter for clarification by the Said board.
I suppose that procedure would be proper, but does it not indicate the ridiculous position in which you place the magistrate. He has to impose a penalty upon a party as to whom he has heard no evidence, yet he must go back to this board-for clarification of the things he should have been told in the first instance. Then to further confuse me I find this in subsection (6):
The board may appeal from the decision or judgment of a magistrate.
In my view the board would not have anything to appeal. It would decide who was guilty or who was innocent. The board could not impose a penalty, and if no penalty was imposed what difference would it make? The position would be exactly the same as before. In my view the fact that the board could

Industrial Relations
appeal the decision of the magistrate would render the magistrate almost powerless. Where would you go if your appeal was granted? Certainly you would not go back to the same magistrate. You would have to go to a higher court.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this bill would do away with the very foundation of unionism. Certainly in my judgment it would put an end to all forms of collective bargain' ing. Suppose this bill passed and a matter came up for collective bargaining between the workers and the company. If they knew this procedure would be followed, neither side would want to reach a decision, and then a conciliation board would have to deal with the matter. It would make no difference which way the board decided; the other party ' would feel aggrieved and would bring the matter before the government, either this government or any other. Then it would become a political football; and I do not think that is the best solution for our problems in labour relations. I believe collective bargaining would break down entirely, and for that reason I am afraid I must oppose this measure. I believe one of the most sacred rights labour has gained over all these years is the right of collective bargaining. I agree that in some cases disputes between labour and management have dragged out for weeks and months, perhaps for more than a year, without reaching a final decision. I think some arrangement should be made under which these decisions must be given within a certain period of time; otherwise that situation will endanger industrial relations in this country.
Having said this much, Mr. Speaker, I do not think I need say more; but I shall have to vote against the bill.

The point I want to make is that there are two objections to the present procedures as far as the trade union movement is concerned. The first is that under the act the offending party cannot be taken

to court without the consent of the minister. Surely that is not the ordinary procedure in law. Surely an offence under the law is an offence, and a person has the right to take the other party to court when an offence occurs. He should not have to wait until the Minister of Labour decides whether or not he may go to court. In my opinion that is not the way British law, or for that matter Canadian law, is administered.

I do not know as to that. The minister can catch me very easily when he asks about something about which perhaps neither of us knows anything. He knows I cannot say that is not the case, because I do not know. I have seen those tricks played before.
During the present session I have heard strong demands made on several occasions in this house that we should change the law that now prevents a person bringing the crown into court without the consent of the crown. Surely if that should be the case when the crown is concerned it should not be different in regard to organizations which under this act are considered as individuals. Now let us look at section 46 of the old act. In my view it is rather strange that the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) should take the worst of the sections that are proposed to be repealed in order to show why they should not be repealed. Section 46 reads:
(1)	No prosecution for an offence under this act shall be instituted except with the consent in writing of the minister.
That is the Minister of Labour.
(2)	A consent by the minister indicating that he has consented to the prosecution of a person named therein for an offence under this act alleged to have been committed, or in the case of a continuing offence, alleged to have commenced, on a date therein set out, shall be a sufficient consent for the purposes of this section to the prosecution of the said person for any offence under this act permitted by or commencing on the said date.
As a matter of fact here the Minister of Labour is acting as a judge of the law he is administering. If he says there is no offence, there is no offence, no matter how aggrieved one party to the dispute may feel. He never has an opportunity to take the other party to court and find out whether or not he has a case unless the minister consents. We had a case of that kind a couple of years ago, when two boards of conciliation appointed by the minister reported in terms as explicit as they possibly could that the employing company was responsible for the trouble. I am not sure whether or not the minister

was asked for leave to prosecute, but there was no prosecution, though in my opinion court proceedings should have been undertaken.

I disagree fundamentally with my hon. friends in the thought that you can negotiate labour agreements on the floor of the House of Commons. That was tried in Germany, and at the very moment it is being tried in France. My mind goes back to my old friend, Sam Gompers, who said, "The truth is still the truth, it does not matter what year it is." He said:
I want to tell you, socialists, that I have studied your philosophy; read your works upon economics, and not the meanest of them; studied your standard works, both in English and German-have not only read, but studied them. I have heard your orators and watched the work of your movement the world over. I have kept close watch upon your doctrines for thirty years; have been closely associated with many of you and know how you think and what you propose. I know, too, what you have up your sleeve. And I want to say that I am entirely at variance with your philosophy. I declare it to you, X am not only at variance with your doctrines, but with your philosophy. Economically, you are unsound; socially, you are wrong; industrially, you are an impossibility.
Now, that is a quotation from the proceedings of a convention of the American Federation of Labor held at Boston in 1903.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Rowe, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Thatcher.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe about fifteen minutes of my time remains. At six o'clock, I was speaking on

the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Dufiferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), with reference to the immediate calling of an interprovincial conference as well as a meeting of the commonwealth countries and crown colonies to discuss the sterling situation which is causing so much trouble between the dollar countries and the sterling countries. The amendment speaks for itself.
As you know, a dominion-provincial conference could be called immediately. Most of the provinces have recently elected new prime ministers, although some of them are holding elections almost immediately. In my opinion, there is no reason why a dominion-provincial conference should not meet at once. I am surprised that the Prime Minister has not already called such a meeting. As my hon. leader very wisely said, there is no reason why such a conference should not be called immediately. You are going to make a scrap of paper out of the whole British North America Act. You have the cart before the horse. The conference should be held now or never, and now and forever or not at all.
I was referring to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). In it he spoke about calling a commonwealth conference immediately for the purpose of discussing with our best customer, Britain and the dominions and colonies-what? The sterling situation. Are we to toss our best customer clean overboard? She has been our best customer all these years. Hon. members will recall that preferential trade was started by the Liberals themselves. You are not supporting the Liberalism of the past.
As I say, this house should not be a rubber stamp. A great many of the younger members come up from the municipalities. We hope there will no longer be yes-men and nodders in this house. Dear knows we have had them long enough. While I am a party man, and support Conservative principles, I am not a bigoted party man-far from it. I think I have shown that ever since I first entered the house. An immediate conference should be called with the dominions and the crown colonies. All these countries should get together and map out a program so that we shall not lose our best customer. I do hope that something will be done about it.
In this debate reference has been made to many matters. During the debate on human rights and also on March 24, 1938-hon. members will recall that date-before the second war started, I said almost the same thing. I do not agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) who said there is no great danger of a war for five years. He corrected that the other day. When you consider

this fact, as I have already said, thanks to Russia the world is faced with two kinds of warfare. One is the atomic bomb which has been perfected by the United States. The Soviet union has devised a more powerful instrument, the cold, brazen, weaponless war and she conquers without destruction. By this method of warfare ten satellite countries have been subjugated and put behind the iron curtain. Let us face the facts and let the public know the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth about this problem. This should be read into the remarks of the Prime Minister the other day. They have got all these countries now behind the iron curtain, and under the threat of aggression they will have the entire world, including those countries of the UNO, in a restless fear of destruction. There is something new in warfare-this struggle for survival. This is only a war of camouflage and it lulls us into a false sense of security in the western country. This cold war and its technique is brilliant as applied by the communists. They know that fear is what scares the satellite countries. They have scuttled pretty nearly the whole of Europe and the rest take it for granted and have taken it for granted until recently. That is the situation which should be faced. There may be trouble in time. For that reason I am of the opinion that the Prime Minister was altogether wrong when he said that there would be five years without war.
I can say this, as I said before: democracy never dies; it perishes from neglect. Militant communism is on the march westward. I want to emphasize the very grave danger this country is in at the present time, as well as this continent and the whole world. Not since the days of Munich has the world outlook been so depressing. Not since the days of the barbarian invasion has Christian civilization faced such a menace as the ruthless advance of communism. These are times that try men's souls. The communists have overrun the Balkan states. Yesterday it was Poland and Austria. Today it is Czechoslovakia and Finland; tomorrow it may be Italy, China, Spain or France. Nations that have experienced the brutality of oppression are now experiencing the cruelty and horror of soviet nightmares. "Their fate", says H. H. Schlact, an American, "will be ours unless we wake up right now. In one generation our dauntless manhood has bled twice and many of them have died on foreign battlefields. They fought to destroy the roots of the insatiable ambitions of fiendish tyrants who sought to enslave humanity."
It is sad to contemplate that after such terrible conflicts we should be faced with such grave events. Russia has the largest 45781-73i
The Budget-Mr. Church army and the largest air force. She does not maintain this mighty military machine for defence; for no one threatens her. She maintains this mighty armada for aggression and attack and conquest. Russia will attack us when she thinks we are weak. She will never attack us if we are strong. While our lawmakers talk, ponder and debate our national security, Russia is relentlessly weaving her web of intrigue and violence wherever she can obtain a foothold. She challenges our physical courage. She challenges our moral fortitude. She challenges our culture and our church. Our democratic way of life is threatened by communist concepts.
Let us sound the clarion call for national defence. Let us summon every true Canadian, every Britisher and American, to fight for national defence. There is little time left; there is no time for timidity. To be free we must be strong. Preparedness is not a war policy but an insurance policy for peace.
In the debate on foreign policy in the British House of Commons Mr. Churchill distinctly said that he never consented to what was done by inviting Russia to come in on the Pacific ten days before Japan collapsed. He never consented to that. That was the idea of the United States. What did she do? Russia was invited in, although Japan was already beaten. This is all referred to in the debates of the British House of Commons on July 21, 1949, and takes up sixty pages of Hansard. I am sorry I have not time to read it tonight. Russia went in there. At that time she had half a million troops in Manchuria. She has now overrun the whole of Asia. She has China and many other places.
I now wish to refer to the Bell Telephone matter. I have about five minutes of time left to deal with that particular matter. A committee of the House of Commons considered this matter two years ago. As a Conservative I strongly opposed the Bell Telephone bill in the house. I was the only one who opposed it on division when the bill was passed. The time has come for the government to be represented by counsel before that body. I remember away back when I was a young alderman in council in 1909 Hon. Mr. Justice Mabee, chairman of the railway board, heard the case at the city hall. At that time the board of control would not do anything about it, and as a young alderman I took the case myself before Mr. Justice Mabee. What did he do? He issued a flat rate for greater Toronto. Citizens were paying as high for telephone bills as $185 a year for business phones, and $95 to $100 for resident phones in the suburbs. Mr. Justice Mabee passed a flat rate for the whole of greater Toronto. He was once a great Liberal and

The Budget-Mr. Gillis a great chairman. I have every confidence in the judges, but you need somebody who will take over and do what the late Mr. Justice Mabee did. We have another opportunity of taking up these matters. I do say that the government should be represented by counsel before the board of transport commissioners when this case is heard. They should oppose the rate; they should oppose any increase. I moved in committee that there be no increase for three years. The workingman will not be able to have a phone-no one will be able to have one. Their stock was at 140 and it went to 183. Then it was split five for one and was quoted at 25. Now it is 42J-and you can see the results.
It has only been in Ontario and Quebec where they have any jurisdiction, because the other provinces have their own telephone systems-and have made a success of it. I say in conclusion that the case should be fought, because these increases are going to have a serious effect. I can remember when the hon. gentleman who used to represent the constituency of Davenport, and I, pointed out that in the villages and towns of western Ontario signs stating "Closed Until Monday" were posted. I pointed out that the telephone system, was part of the post office department in England, and that over there they had boxes on the street from which a person could phone for a taxi. And it was as a result of this action, along with that of the hon. member who used to represent that constituency, Davenport, Mr. MacNicol, that we got telephone boxes on our streets in our cities and towns.
For the reasons I have stated I say the government should be represented by counsel and should oppose any increases for three years. There should be no increase at all. The public cannot pay it, and it simply means that the working class in Canada will not have phones-or if they do have them, will have them only at prohibitive prices.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall try to stick as closely as possible to the matters coming within the scope of the budget. I listened to it on a previous occasion and heard it discussed. I am not unmindful of the fact that since that time there has been an election at which the government was returned to power with a substantial majority. Nevertheless I believe considerable criticism can be levelled at the budget, as such.
The first point I should like to make is one we have made on many occasions, namely that the budget as brought in by the minister is merely a bookkeeping statement for the past year. We have recommended from time to time-and I repeat it tonight-that in a country which has just been through a war,

and which is still in the process of bringing its economy back to a peacetime basis, where there is considerable unemployment throughout the country, in addition to bringing in a statement showing expenditures and anticipated surpluses the minister should also bring in a capital budget. The government has taken the position from time to time that, while it does not agree with the principle of having the government in business, where free enterprise failed they have been prepared to take up the slack. They have been doing that to some extent, but not in the manner in which we would like to see it done.
I say the minister should be setting aside large sums from surpluses which have accumulated from budget to budget since the war. He should be picking out those spots in Canada where the economy needs a lift, and where the edge has been taken off industry. He should be presenting to the house a plan to be effective from coast to coast whereby, although he might not step on the corns of free enterprise, he would take action where free enterprise has failed to make good where it felt it was not profitable to invest money. Thereby he would give us a national plan across the country under which we would spend in given areas certain sums from our surplus, to enable the people in different parts of the country which are considered depressed to make plans for the future.
This would give employment offices an opportunity to plan employment. In my opinion that kind of budget is absolutely necessary. I notice that in some provinces, particularly in Nova Scotia, that kind of action is now being taken. In addition to the regular budget of the last session of the Nova Scotia legislature, the premier introduced one just as I have described.
This is one respect in which the minister's department has fallen down. He did not consult with the other departments-public works, mines and resources, or any of the others-nor has he given us any idea of what the government had in mind in the depressed areas.
The second point to which I would direct the minister's thoughts is connected with the removal of the 8 per cent sales tax on fuel oil. The assumption by most people is that they are going to receive the benefit immediately of an 8 per cent reduction in the cost of fuel oil. I believe I am safe in saying that the majority of distributors, those who sell to the consumers, never knew there was a sales tax. So far as I can gather it went directly to the oil companies. Whether that saving is going to be passed on to the consumer remains to be seen. I suggest that some time before the end of the session the minister should make some decision in

this matter. I believe the assumption in his department was that in taking off the 8 per cent sales tax the saving would be passed on to the consumer. Today however there is no indication of that, and some decision should be made in the matter. I shall have more to say about it at a later time.
May I now direct a few words to the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer), who spoke in the house last evening. He is a new member, and as 1 sat and listened to him I noted that most of his discussion was directed to ridiculing other groups not seated with the government. He made some disparaging remarks about splinter groups, and in his view it seems that it was because everyone was so far off the mark and so politically unwise that we now have this huge majority on the government benches.
Because he is a new member I forgive him for much of what he said. Before he is here long however he will find that the House of Commons is one of the broadest forums it has ever been my privilege or will ever be his privilege to attend. It is a forum in which one's measure is taken rather quickly. If one is inclined to be small or mean in his approach to problems in the house, or in personal attacks, he does not get very far in the House of Commons.
I thought that the hon. member's references last night to splinter groups were uncalled for. Let me remind him that, as far back as one can go in the records of history, one finds that it was the small groups, who were not self-seeking, who were not looking for something for themselves, but who were pioneering for social reform, who have been responsible for all the reforms in the history of the world.
It was only yesterday afternoon we sat in the House of Commons, with hon. members from the other place and the public at large -among whom was the hon. member for Maple Creek, I have no doubt-and listened to and applauded the Prime Minister of India. He was a splinter, he stood alone for a long time in that country. He spent over eight years in British prisons because he fought British imperialism. But despite that he carried on, he advanced his ideas and stuck by his principles. Today he is the oak tree of India, the man who will perhaps have the greatest influence on the future of the world.
I would remind the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) that that kind of approach in this House of Commons does not go down too well. We respect everyone's opinion in a matter of this kind, and sometimes I even agree with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). I think he has the right to hold whatever opinion he wishes.
The Budget-Mr. Gillis
Last evening the hon. member thought that it was because of political immaturity and a nonsensical approach to things that the government was so large and the opposition so small. I would remind the hon. member that it is not good enough to get up and make statements of that kind in this house if he has not the necessary facts to put on the record to support them. When I went upstairs I picked up a western newspaper which I am sure is quite friendly to the government, a newspaper that would not want to put out propaganda. A report in this newspaper refers to figures put out by the dominion bureau of statistics which show that farm income in 1949 had increased by 14-7 per cent over the figure for the same period last year. I should like to read a few of these figures which might indicate why the government was able to influence the western vote in the last election. I am not suggesting that anyone was bribed, but I do suggest that these figures are thought-provoking. The article reads:
Canadian fanners realized a cash income of $1,056,500,000 from the sale of farm products during the first six months of this year, according to preliminary estimates released by the dominion bureau of statistics.
This was 14-7 per cent over the 1948 cash income of $921,400,000 for the same period and an increase of 45-9 per cent over the $724,300,000 received during the first half of 1947.
In addition, supplementary payments amounting to more than $9,000,000 were paid out, during the first six months of this year under the provisions of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, to farmers in the drought-stricken areas of the prairie provinces. This compares with nearly $10,000,000 in 1947 and more than $15,000,000 in 1948.
The first six months of this year would bring us up to June. The western farmers have received these benefits under prairie farm assistance, P.F.R.A., and all the other A.A.'s they have and I suggest that if everyone in Canada was treated as fairly by way of bonuses and subsidies and supplementary payments-it must be remembered that a large proportion of those particular payments went to the province from which the hon. member for Maple Creek comes-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps if they took as many chances things would be different.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member is a reeve now, so he should watch his dignity.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Labour never takes chances.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not suggesting or insinuating anything; I am merely putting a few facts on the record and will allow hon. members to judge for themselves whether it was political immaturity and nonsensical arguments on the part of the splinter groups or irresponsible action that is responsible for the large majority the government has in the house. Or, on

The Budget-Mr. Gillis the other hand, was it the spending of the taxpayers' money in certain areas where the government was weak that had the greatest influence in sending to this house a large number of Liberal members from the prairie provinces? I ask the hon. member for Maple Creek to think that over.
From time to time we hear arguments that we are prosperous, that we are going forward, that we have a decentralized economy, that there is no monopoly and that everyone has an equal opportunity. That argument was advanced on several occasions during the war and has been since. It was said that there was a great levelling off of income in Canada and our provinces were assured equal treatment in the distribution of the national income. I should like to focus attention on this for a few minutes, not in a critical way but merely to provide some food for thought.
I have in my hand a little booklet that was issued in 1943 by the National Liberal Federation of Canada. This book contained a question and answer set-up which was attractively done and nicely worded. I intend to quote very little of it, but there are parts that have a bearing on the subject of commercial failures to which I should like to direct attention. The soldier was being asked what he wanted to come back to, what kind of Canada he wanted to come back to, and he is supposed to make this answer:
I remember my father telling me how the little business he tried to start collapsed during the inflation of the twenties, and he had to begin all over again.
Then this statement is made:
That will be avoided this time. To help pay for the war as it is being fought, your government has made such laws as 100 per cent tax on excess profits, heavy income taxes on large and medium incomes, compulsory savings on all taxable incomes, borrowings through six victory loans and through the sale of war savings certificates.
That was correct at that time. The statement continues:
And your government didn't stop there. Price ceilings and controls have held down the cost of living, so that when you get back into civilian life you won't be shunted into a topsy-turvy world of high prices and uncertain values.
That was in 1943 when all the machinery described in that booklet was in operation. It worked at that time and it could have worked in the post-war period. When the soldier came out of the service he remembered that he had accepted literally the statements and promises which had been made in the literature distributed to him. Many of these boys went into small businesses. They took their gratuities and credits and set themselves up. I have in my hand some figures from the dominion bureau of statistics which indicate the trend in commercial failures in this country.
IMr. Gillis.]
Mind you, it is not Canada Packers who are failing. It is not Dominion Steel and Coal or International Nickel who are failing. It is the little fellow, the man who did not have much capital behind him who has been swallowed up by the octopus that is able to squeeze him dry. I know some of these boys who have taken what they had saved during the war to go into little businesses but who have been squeezed out because of a lack of capital. Here is the trend in commercial failures in this country as indicated by this article, which reads:
Commercial failures in the first half of 1949 were the highest in number for the similar period since 1941, while estimated liabilities amounted to $8,725,009, a gain of 22-5 per cent over 1948 and "the highest for the first six months of any year since 1934 when the economy was just starting to recover from its lowest levels," according to the dominion bureau of statistics.
Nearly all branches of business showed increases in failures. For example, as compared with last year, trade and manufactures increased 14 and 21 per cent respectively. Furthermore, all areas, except Ontario, shared the increase.
Maritime Failures Double
"There were eleven failures in the maritimes as compared with six last year," the D.B.S. report states. "Quebec showed an increase of 57 to record a post-war high of 380, while the number of failures in Ontario declined from 67 to 59 in the same comparison.
Then the article deals with the prairie provinces. That is not a good trend and, as I pointed out, I think legislation should be enacted to halt it. I mentioned a moment ago that many of our service personnel were encouraged to invest what capital they had in small businesses. The promise was made that the price control machinery and other such machinery as we had during the war would protect them, and would if it were still in existence. The right of the government to fix prices and regulate production and the allocation of materials and supplies to some extent would have protected them, but we did not live up to the promise. When we threw that machinery in the discard on the cessation of hostilities we left price fixing and the distribution of goods and services across the country in the hands of people who have sufficient control over everything that is produced and distributed in Canada to say who is and who is not going to get it, what price you are going to pay for it, and what the mark-up will be.
With that kind of machinery small businesses, which we should be encouraging and protecting, are gradually being pushed out of the picture. As the figures I have quoted are official, inasmuch as they come from a government bureau, I suggest that the minister should take the matter under consideration and try to devise some machinery

whereby small businesses with limited capital may be enabled to remain in operation, because that is the kind of business that we want to encourage in Canada.
The next point to which I should like to draw the attention of the minister and the government is the matter of the distribution of income. The hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) suggested that income was distributed fairly equally across the country, and that the government had achieved a balance in the whole economy. I have some figures here which also come from the dominion bureau of statistics. They have to do with per capita income by provinces and indicate the standard of living. While it is not an accurate measurement, nevertheless it is a pretty good indication of what the standard of living is in the various provinces.
I should like to point out for the benefit of hon. members that the national income of Canada is far from being equally distributed and, mind you, the trend is downward since the end of the war. I wish to cite a few figures. In British Columbia and the Yukon, for example, per capita income has declined by 9 per cent from 1945 to 1948. Alberta has gone up by 14 per cent. Saskatchewan has gone up by 13 per cent. Manitoba is up by 3 per cent. Ontario has gone down 11 per cent. Quebec has gone down 3 per cent. New Brunswick has gone down 9 per cent. Nova Scotia has gone down 15 per cent, and Prince Edward Island has gone down 9 per cent. This is a matter which I should particularly like to draw to the attention of members from the maritime provinces. I have not the figures for Newfoundland but I imagine they are even worse. In 1948 the per capita income for British Columbia and the Yukon was $661, Alberta $643, Saskatchewan $601, Manitoba $610, Ontario $694, Quebec $506, New Brunswick $410, Nova Scotia $440, and Prince Edward Island $354.
These figures indicate to me that the per capita income of the maritime provinces is approximately 33 per cent below that of the rest of Canada. That means that the standard of living in those provinces is 33 per cent lower than it is in the rest of Canada.

speechtext:
That is the per capita income and figures do not lie. I suggest that there must be serious planning by the government to increase the standard of living of the
The Budget-Mr. Gillis maritime provinces. Mind you, we are not asking for charity because that part of the country at the time of confederation was the most prosperous section of Canada. As I pointed out a few nights ago, since confederation there have been over 200 industries siphoned off from the maritime provinces and centralized in Quebec and Ontario, and that trend continued right up until 1943. Many of them were not small industries. One that was shifted into Montreal in 1943 was a plant that had operated previously at Trenton, Nova Scotia, and had employed some 1,600 men. It had been operating there for approximately thirty years. The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Carroll), who was on the bench at that time, wrote a report on that particular operation which was a strong condemnation of governments which would permit the siphoning off of an industry of that kind. He stated that if one-third of the money spent on moving it into Montreal had been spent on modernizing the plant where it was it would have been a better operation where it was than in Montreal.
When I say we are not asking for charity, we are asking you, by establishing subsidiary industries in that section of the country, to try to give us back at least 50 per cent of the industries that were stolen from us. That is not charity; it is restoration.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Restitution.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Or restitution. There is a way that it can be done. The government is doing it now to some extent but someone else reaps the profits rather than the people of the maritime provinces. I said a moment ago that I would say something about coal. I listened to a discussion in the house about abolishing the smoke nuisance in the city of Toronto. I heard the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) say that the intention of the railways is to replace, as rapidly as they can, steam engines with diesel engines burning oil. One of the basic industries of Nova Scotia is coal, and one of the largest customers for that coal is the Canadian National Railways. In effect the minister said that as soon as they can do it that market will be taken away. The development of the use of oil in Canada from coast to coast definitely shows that for steamships, railroads and domestic purposes oil is the coming thing in the near future.
Well, while you are solving that problem you are creating another: what are you going to do with the coal industry? I suggest the time has arrived when the government should be examining the possibility of other uses for coal rather than just burning it and letting it go up in smoke. The oil resources of this continent are not unlimited;

The Budget-Mr. Gillis anyone who examines the matter closely will see that. With the developments in the air, in which fuel oils will be necessary, and with the present trend to use oil for everything else, the resources of this country can be depleted very quickly. So I suggest that at this time the government should be probing the possibilities of producing oil from coal. The whole industrial set-up of Germany was based on the extraction of the byproducts of a very inferior grade of coal, but very little is being done in that field in this country. During the past year or two the government have spent a great deal of money on research in other directions, but nothing has been done about research in that field, which goes to the very base of the economy of this or any other country. If tomorrow the United States decided to keep in their own country the twenty-six or twenty-eight million tons of coal we import every year, within a couple of months practically all our industries would be tied up. We do not have the fuel ourselves. Britain's big problem since the end of the war has been lack of fuel. When Henry Wallace came back from Europe two years ago, when the Marshall plan was being talked about, he made the statement that if we could send fifty, sixty or a hundred million tons of coal to Germany in order that they might get their own plants and factories into operation, that would be the best contribution we could make. Apparently we are not going to appreciate this problem until we run smack up against it some time.
In other fields the government is spending a good deal of money on research, and rightly so. I am not objecting to it, but I am going to make a comparison. In the development of atomic energy and jet engines, on the national research council, on agriculture, fisheries, forests, aerial photography and that kind of thing, the government spent $81,857,000 on research in 1947-48. But to provide for the fabrication, erection and equipment of hydrogenation plants to do the kind of research I am suggesting, the bureau of mines spent $4,500 on an engineering design. The expenditure for research in that field actually made in those two years was $3,090, which shows that the problem is absolutely not considered by those who are in a position to have that sort of research carried on. With the oil development in Alberta the coal industry of that province, which is represented here by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), will be nearly wiped out within the next year or two.
It is true that these are matters coming under provincial jurisdiction, yet I say it is time the national government began to pay some attention to that field, because

the coal industry of this country is a great national asset. It can be used for many purposes; and I leave that thought with those who are responsible for it.
Now I want to offer what I believe would be an immediate solution for the problems of Nova Scotia, and what I think would give the maritime provinces generally a very great lift. I suggest that the government should be considering the immediate expansion of the steel plant at Sydney. I am not guessing on this; I have my statistics again. Iron ore in the United States, where they carry on some terrific steel operations, is running out. The greatest iron ore deposits in the world are over here in Ungava. I could quote statements indicating that before very long the major steel plants of the United States will be shifting to the eastern seaboard, to New Hampshire and Maine, in order to be close to the raw materials in Newfoundland, which they pretty well control now, by remote control, through front companies in Canada.
This government has given a great deal of money, by way of subsidies and grants, to the operating steel industry in Canada; that is, to Algoma, Stelco and Dosco, which are supreme in the field of steel. I have all the figures here, and I am going to summarize them. From 1939 to 1948 inclusive government subsidies to the iron and steel industry amounted to $51,776,483.65. That is not peanuts. Special depreciation allowance to Stelco, Algoma and Dosco from 1939 to 1948 inclusive amounted to $14,128,447.40. Net profits after taxes of the three operating companies I have mentioned, for the same period, were $58,981,586. The operation of these major steel plants has been quite costly to the taxpayers of this country; but the figures I have just given show that if it had not been for government assistance these companies would have had an operating deficit of some $7 million during that period.
What does this indicate? To me it indicates that an industry in which the Canadian people have such an investment-because after all that is our money-should have some measure of government management. There is no reason why a board of directors we never see, responsible to no one but themselves, should be spending this amount of public money in that industry and taking those profits because they are subsidized to that extent, without the government having some say in the spending of the money and the expansion of the industry.
The problem is not fabricated steel but raw steel. At that very point we have coal, and we have the iron ore just a few miles away across the gulf. We have the boats to carry the ore. Why are not the facilities expanded

for the making of raw steel? Why are we now, under whatever measure of steel control we still have, compelling Dosco to ship that raw steel back to Stelco and to Montreal for fabrication? Why are we not going after the overseas market? There will be a market for raw steel overseas for a long time to come. The logical market for that part of the country is the overseas market; and I suggest that with this amount of public money invested in that industry the production of raw steel should be stepped up. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is a man for whom I have very high regard, a man who has carried a terrific load during the last ten years. On a good many occasions I have heard him say that steel was our main bottleneck, and that the production of raw steel would have to be increased. Why is that not being done? Why is not the government in a position to say to the operating company at the Sydney end of it, particularly, that they shall do nothing but turn out raw steel? Why is the government not in a position to say that the plant must be expanded? The government is paying out enough money, so let us step up the facilities and go after the overseas market.
My time is drawing to a close. I just wanted to leave these few suggestions with the government; but before I conclude I want to say this. During this debate, I have heard considerable discussion on the matter of trade. Much of the emphasis was on our export markets. A country that exports one-third of its total production will have to have export markets; there is no doubt about that. But what about the home market? What are we doing about that? I suggest that before any country commences advising the people in some other country what they should do, it should put its own house in order. There are ways by which we could create a greater internal consumption in Canada.
One of the things upon which I should like to focus attention is that of increasing our old age pensions. In this country there are approximately 200,000 old age pensioners. These people now receive $30 per month, with a supplement of $10 per month where there are extenuating circumstances. Why could we not step that up to $50 per month? Why could we not lower the age to the minimum that has been suggested, 65 and 60? Immediately someone will say that the bill for this would be tremendous. Fifty dollars per month is not a large sum of money, as anyone who is living in Ottawa knows. It will just buy the necessities of life for an old lady or an old gentleman. It will buy a bite to eat, and that is all.
The Budget-Mr. Gillis
If that additional $20 per month were given without a means test, it would mean those people would have $20 per month more to spend. There are 200,000 of them. All this money would go towards buying the essentials of life. The lowering of the age limit to 65 would lay off men and make employment for younger people who could produce more. In the final analysis, the younger people should be kept in the fields in which productivity is necessary. If we did that we would not be facing the problems that we are facing today, with no one responsible for the aged or the charitable contribution that the old age pension has become. You have to be old to get it, three score and ten. Then there is the means test, of course. I believe that is something we can do. The money would not go out of this country. It would be spent in this country. It would create employment for the younger people, who would produce more. It would start to turn the wheels of industry.
The thing which we must keep in mind is that it is necessary to keep up the standard of our people. If we are going to weather the storm that is ahead, we must have full production. All this talk one hears about communism, bolshevism, and all these other isms, does not bother me. I am not particular about the tags, and I never was. I like to see things done. If we can show the people in the outside world that our system is working, our people are happy and, basically, things are not bad, there is no need to fear any other philosophy. It is the little irritations, such as the means test in old age pensions, that keep the people upset. Those things make it easy for any demagogue who wants to come in and sell his line of chatter to them.
I have not sufficient time to go into this question of devaluation. I want to say emphatically, however, that so far as devaluation is concerned Britain was forced into it by the United States in order to sell her produce there and in this country. The devaluation of the pound was a last desperate move for survival on the part of the United Kingdom. It did not solve anything. The devaluation of our dollar by ten per cent raises by that amount the cost of everything that comes in from the United States. The minister should not be surprised. He has been devaluing the Canadian dollar since 1945-since 1939, in fact-in terms of purchasing power. In the field of food, in which about eighty per cent of the income of the lower income groups is spent, the dollar has been devalued by about fifty per cent. In the over-all picture, it has been devalued by about thirty-five per cent. In the field of housing-well, it has gone out of existence.

The Budget-Mr. A. Gauthier We should not be surprised or shocked, therefore, that Britain has been forced to make that move in order to assure economic survival.
I notice, Mr. Speaker, that you are getting restless. I do not want to impose upon the house. I hope the minister will read my remarks in Hansard and attempt to correct some of the injustices I have been trying to describe.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this being the first time that I have had the honour and privilege of speaking in this house, it is fitting that I should do so in French. I wish to take this opportunity to congratulate you upon your accession to the high office which you now hold. I also wish to congratulate particularly the Deputy Speaker of the house who so worthily represented my constituency during the last four years before the present parliament was called.
It is my heavy responsibility to take his place as the representative of my constituency. I trust that bearing in mind the high standard which he set in parliament during those years, and fully aware of the responsibilities of my office, which I have accepted entirely, I shall not be the cause of too much disappointment.
Geographically speaking, the constituency I have the honour to represent is situated in the north of the province of Quebec, forming a semicircle around the great lake St. John. Father Jean de Quen set up the cross there more than three centuries ago.
The population of the constituency, almost entirely of French descent, is half agricultural and half industrial. The hydroelectric development at Maligne island and the imminent harnessing of the Peribonca river portend a great industrial future for my district. The farming community, sound and intelligent, has kept the best French traditions. It is a fact that the highest average number of children per family for the whole of Canada is to be found at Notre Dame d'Hebertville, a fine agricultural centre. That half the population of that locality should be of school age is therefore not surprising.
Aluminum production of Maligne island and the pulp mills of River Bend bring well deserved earnings to an industrious and law-abiding class of workers. At both latter points, the English-speaking people of my riding live in perfect harmony with the French-speaking population. This is a living

example and a concrete symbol of that unity which must and does exist throughout Canada.
Lumbering, related and subordinate to the paper industry, is generally prosperous though at the present time there is a rather marked drop in employment, due to the uncertain British market. Moreover, pulp companies, having accumulated substantial reserves, have seen fit this year to do much less wood-cutting, hence the considerable rise in unemployment. It might be felt that unemployment insurance will come to the rescue of these men in their temporary difficulties but such is not the case. This timber industry does not fall within the jurisdiction of the commission and those who are deprived of their usual livelihood are in urgent need of help.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that the government is not responsible for a situation like this one. I am confident however that once it is made conversant with the facts, the government will, in order to remedy the situation, immediately undertake certain public works which were planned during the past few years. Such projects already exist in many parishes of my county, particularly in St. Joseph d'Alma.
Up to now my requests have been favourably received by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) and I wish to thank him for the first results obtained.
Since lumbermen are not exempt from the fluctuations of employment, they should receive the attention of the Department of Labour. The department should, immediately and without taking into account the representations of certain pulp and paper companies, apply the Unemployment Insurance Act to the lumbering industry. That would prevent a recurrence of what is going on at present.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about my elderly constituents. Most industries seem to have made it a rule to turn down requests for work from people over 65 years of age. If men can no longer earn a living at 65, then this is the very age at which the government should grant them a pension, so they will not come to want. All old people should be paid a pension without the means test-as is being done now in the case of family allowances-or without sacrificing any nest egg they have set aside for their old age.
Mr. Speaker, the members of all parties in the house are unanimous in proclaiming the autonomy of our country, both in the national

and international spheres. But we should assert our sovereignty in the economic as well as in the political field.
Our trade policy must be resolutely and firmly directed towards Canada's best interests, even if it means the sacrifice of traditional markets often preserved for sentimental rather than practical reasons. The Geneva agreements and the Annecy negotiations are a step in the right direction. In this respect, I am happy to congratulate the government while urging that this policy be pursued still further for we cannot always expect to link two great economic powers. Fortunately, the policy of the government has put us in a better position to play the important part for which we are fitted in the field of trade.
Mr. Speaker, I know that in the minds of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and of the members of his cabinet, there is no room for any inferiority complex of a political or economical nature; it is in that spirit that I supported the government during the last election.
I do not belong to that generation whose only interest is to magnify the glories of the past, but rather do I belong to that generation which looks to the future, which, while it jealously guards the legacy left by its forebears, is anxious to enrich, improve, and develop it.
For this reason, Mr. Speaker, because the present government is going in that direction, I have every faith in the future of my constituency and in the destiny of my country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, being a Liberal and a democrat at the same time I think my first words should be to congratulate those who were elected yesterday in the eight by-elections held in Canada. In a democracy everyone is entitled to his own political opinion, and in respect of their political platforms I think we should congratulate them and convey to them our best wishes for success in the course of their political lives.
Tonight I want to say a few words on an industry operating in my own riding. I hope that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) will give my request his best attention. In February, 1947, I wrote the minister a letter asking him to do something on the St. Lawrence river in order that the ferry from Lotbiniere to Deschambault, my home town, would have greater facility in carrying fertilizer produced in my constituency. This fertilizer is produced by the Deschambault Quarry Corporation of St.
The Budget-Mr. P. Gauthier Marc des Carrieres. It is called the Deschambault Quarry Corporation because this parish was a part of Deschambault, and the limestone of Deschambault was used by this corporation and built up a fine reputation for St. Marc des Carrieres. The company erected a plant and started to produce fertilizer from limestone dust. Its trademark is "Calco". This company has been distributing Calco for twenty-five years. Every year for seven months of the year it has been shipping around fifty to sixty carloads of Calco a day. They are making improvements so as to be able to ship in the province of Quebec and into Ontario nearly a hundred carloads a day. In each carload is forty tons, therefore quite a large amount of Calco is distributed to the farmers of the district. This company is distributing on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, in the county of the Solicitor General (Mr. Lapointe), the county of Nicolet, the county of Quebec, and on the north shore in the counties next to mine, and has been shipping into Ontario and the lower part of the south shore of Quebec.
As I said, the company has been shipping around fifty or sixty carloads a day. To that must be added the hundreds of trucks which carry this fertilizer onto the farmers' land during seven months of the year. If I ask for improvements, if I ask that the channel be dredged from the north shore of Deschambault up to the St. Lawrence to allow the ferry to transport this Calco, it is a request that should be granted. The letter which I sent to the minister on February 18, 1947, contained all that I have said about the Calco producing company of St. Marc des Carrieres. The minister answered on March 5, saying that a survey by his engineering staff was to be made, and he gave me the result of the survey on April 21, 1947. He said the cost would be around $400,000. That is a large amount of money to spend. But when we think of the thousands of farmers using that fertilizer so as to make the land more productive I believe we would agree that the cost is not too high. I should hope that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) might see that this work is performed next year.
I did not make any election promises. I have been working at this for a few years, because I have known it was absolutely necessary. I know my farmers want it, and that the farmers in the south shore counties along the St. Lawrence want it, too. I believe it is a necessity, and that the Liberal government should continue to give farmers the facilities they need to carry out their farming operations, and those operations of production necessary for the benefit of the Canadian people.

The Budget-Mr. P. Gauthier
In the budget we see that the government is making many grants for many purposes including public health, research, physical fitness, scholarships, and scholarships to help the medical man attain a specialty in some branch or other of the medical field. For these reasons I believe I am entitled to speak briefly on a matter concerning which I spoke at the last session of parliament. I refer to the spread and enormous consumption of alcoholic liquors in our country. I know, and I am sure every hon. member knows, that if one wants to cure a patient of any illness or disease, the medical man must attack the evil at its source. If one concentrates his effort on. the same symptoms he errs; he walks in a circle without attaining his goal, which is the betterment of his client.
With the permission of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) I should like to quote what he said in a speech delivered in the House of Commons on March 4, 1949. Speaking with respect to national hygiene he said, as reported at page 1149 of Hansard:
For years X have tried to use the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne as a vehicle to talk to the members, and to try to bring before them the necessity for some action to bring about betterment of health conditions in Canada, and a definite health plan for Canada. For this I offer no apology. It is not so much because of my own interest in these matters as it is that I realize there are conditions in Canada-
And the hon. member proceeded to mention hospitalization and the lack of opportunity for treatment-


that make it a matter which should receive the
attention of all members.
We must recognize today that, with nations as with individuals, we are faced with the fact of the survival of the fittest, and if Canada does not raise the standard of health of her citizens to a maximum equal to that of any other nation she will fall by the wayside in international affairs. We must recognize a nation's health at its full value, not only from the human point of view, but from the economic side as well. We must realize that money spent on health is money saved.
And I allow myself to add that money spent on liquor is money lost. When he says we have to raise the standard of health of our citizens to a point equal to that of any other nation, we have to think that the best way to cure is to prevent, and the best way to prevent is to state bluntly, without any futile attack on anyone, the real situation concerning the spread of alcohol in our country.
Dr. R. G. Bell, who is an authority on alcoholic matters, stated in Toronto on March 2, 1949:
As far as medical science can determine, there is no satisfactory solution for the alcoholic but total abstinence for the rest of his life-
This is a little drastic, but it is true.
-and modem treatment is designed to make this possible.

Let me quote another authority in this connection. In a letter sent to me by Dr. A. M. Campbell of Winnipeg, after I had made a speech in the house, he said:
The menace of the spread of alcoholism to the character and health and future of our young people is one of the great questions of our times, and the means to combat it are so ineffectual.
I think he is right. And if the means are ineffectual, then I do not think everyone is taking the steps necessary to combat the abuse of alcohol in our country. Perhaps hon. members will recall that in a speech I delivered on February 22, 1949, I quoted Dr. Monin who was secretary of the comity of hygiene in France-and this goes back to pre-1900 days. He said:
The truest word ever uttered on this subject remains perhaps that of Bucknill: "The drunkard drinks because he is insane. He is insane because he drinks."
Dr. Monin adds:
Alcohol is a major factor in criminality. The investigations carried out by Mr. Yvernes show that the first principle violated by the drunk man is the respect of officials.
I do not see why a public man can utter sentences like these, and leave every facility to people within their own province to use as much liquor as they want, thus developing a lack of respect for the law, and giving even to children of fifteen years the opportunity to obtain liquor in any liquor dispensary, hotel or grill. If, as Mr. Yvernes said, the first principle violated by the drunken man is the respect of officials, then I do not see why we can talk about the respect we have for authority when we give such wide opportunities to everyone to obtain alcoholic drinks.
You know very well, Mr. Speaker, that a man intoxicated has no will power. I do not see why we are not taking the necessary steps-and I say "we", meaning that public authorities should have an understanding so that they might get together and stop the giving of these facilities to youngsters of fifteen years. Dr. Monin continues:
Then come insults to policemen, destruction of trees, plants, fences, gross indecency, assault and battery, seditious cries, conditional threats, manslaughter through criminal negligence, arson . . .
A tenth of all murders result from bar-room brawls. Of one hundred divorces granted in Denmark 24 are granted on grounds of drunkenness (Magnus Huss).
Dr. Monin says further on:
In the comer of each brain, used to say Moreau (of Tours), madness lies dormant; the main thing is not to bring it to life.
I am using many quotations because I do not think I am qualified to speak directly on this subject. I am not a specialist but I think I should do my utmost to perform my duty as a public man to help Canadians to get rid of this pain in the side, if I may use that

phrase. I should like now to quote the Temperance Advocate, which in turn quotes Mr. William J. Faulkner of the Message magazine of Nashville, Tennessee. Mr. Faulkner is referring to the way in which advertisers are trying to get the attention of the general public in order to increase the sale of liquor, and I quote from the article:
"We need to understand the habits of women and the younger generation. Train your publicity to catch the eye and develop the interest of the younger generation . . . Make youth liquor conscious . . . Make it smart to drink wine. Teach American women to drink." These were slogans adopted at the March, 1935, convention of 49 leaders of the wine and liquor industries in Chicago. And they are really making the younger generation liquor conscious.
It is high time that college presidents, deans, professors, and counselors organized their forces in a scientific attack on the major evil in our society. They must co-operate with the church, the home, the public schools, and the government in an intelligent nation-wide crusade against strong drink.
We in Canada should also co-operate with the church, the home, the public schools, and the governments if they want to, in an intelligent nation-wide crusade against strong drink. I should like to refer now to an article in the Toronto Star of October 12, 1949, by Robert Taylor, the staff correspondent. It reads:
Canadians spent $48 per capita last year for alcohol compared with $28.50 on medical care and death expenses, a survey by the dominion bureau of statistics reveals.
Each Canadian averaged almost as much for tobacco, $24, as for fuel, $27.
And again:
The magnitude of the Canadian booze bill may be gathered by the fact that it was considerably greater than the total amount the federal government spent in the same year on family allowances, war service gratuities, re-establishment credits, rehabilitation benefits, pensions for both wars, war veterans' allowances, unemployment insurance benefits, Prairie Farm Assistance Act benefits and pensions to government employees.
Here are some comparative figures showing the per	capita	expenditures on	different
commodities:
1948	1938
Food	
$215.00	$75.60Clothing	
102.00	34.00Household operations	
78.00	60.50Alcohol	
48.00	15.00
Those increases are worth noting. An article in the Toronto Star of July 4, 1949, states that a hospital is going to be built in Toronto for the treatment of alcoholics. The article states:
The Ontario government is to "get tough" with those who do not observe the liquor laws.
But Ontario has been going right ahead creating alcoholics who will require treatment.
Ontario has been multiplying the liquor outlets which in turn multiply the number of drinkers and thus increase the problems of law administration.
The Budget-Mr. P. Gauthier
What is the use of building hospitals to treat alcoholics when we provide the populace with every facility to obtain alcoholic beverages? If a man or woman succumbs to the lure of alcohol it is very rarely that he or she can overcome the longing without treatment. The main thing is not to start. I should like to quote now from another article which I consider is of great importance. I shall quote this in French and then give the house a general idea of what it says: (Translation):
This article was published in the May, 1941, issue of the Jesuits' review and is entitled "Alcohol and Democracy":
Having been introduced on Tuesday night, Bill 56, amending the Alcoholic Liquor Act was voted on second and third reading by the provincial legislature.
And again:
Such is the true reform awaited with understandable impatience by all the honest citizens of this province and especially the new women voters, wives and mothers, who will judge of its merits by what it does and not by its promises. The new legislation seeks to reimpart to the Lord's day something of its Christian character, and to the night something of its original purpose. It also seeks to lessen the lying power of liquor advertisements, to divest night clubs and hotel rooms of some of their glamour, and finally make enforcement a little more effective. All these points have been won, at least in theory, by the public opinion campaign on behalf of temperance.
(Text):
It is true that a good job was being done against the enormous spread of the use of alcoholic beverages. I think the law should be enforced by the government and an effort made to get the public interested in this question of the sale of alcoholic beverages. In Quebec there have been cases where children of 15 years of age have been sold alcoholic beverages. I quote again: (Translation):
And that in spite of unanimous, energetic and repeated protests from the highest religious authorities, parent associations and Christian labour movements, and in spite of 260,000 affidavits.
(Text):
We are now in the year 1949 and I believe that what that article says is still true. I quote again in French:
(Translation):
In any event a vigorous and intelligent temperance campaign is required more than ever before, so as to uphold the will of the government to prevent abuses and have the law respected, and also to lessen the effects of this shady and evil clause, until it is repealed.
(Text):
I believe in Quebec the law has not been enforced to its full extent, and I hope that the provincial authorities will at last open their eyes and see that the law is fully respected. I have here a letter written by Mr. J. Wilfrid Gaudette, general president of the

The Budget-Mr. P. Gauthier Sacred Heart league, to L'Action Catholique to be found in the issue of March 25, 1949. He has also written repeatedly to the premier of the province of Quebec. I am glad that once in a while a man feels strongly enough about a subject to dare to put his finger on the evil without being afraid of reprisals of any kind from anyone, even from the government itself. Mr. Gaudette says in his letter: (Translation):
For some time past, the Prime Minister has on many occasions, pointed out the need of action as regards law enforcement. In the case of the liquor commission law, it does seem that breaches give rise to much less scruples on the part of authorities.
An inquiry has recently been conducted in parishes about the observance of the liquor law in licensed establishments on Sunday. More than 300 parishes from 60 provincial counties have sent in replies. Over 50 per cent of the latter state that hotels, taverns and licensed establishments are breaking the law by selling liquor at all times on Sunday, in spite of the fact that the law only authorizes the sale of wine and beer between one o'clock in the afternoon and 9 o'clock in the evening, with meals comprising food for a value of at least 40 cents.
That article was published on March 25, 1949, and Mr. Gaudette added:
Law is being transgressed through the sale of liquor to minors. It is being broken through the sale of liquor to drunken people. It is being transgressed also through the sale of liquor without a licence. In the majority of the parishes which have answered our inquiry, it is said that the liquor commission have no control, that the action they do take, if any, is inefficient. When such abuses are reported to the authorities, they reply that those disorders are the result of the original sin. We are no longer at the time of the original sin. We have at least come to the deluge, which floods our province.
We know that each of our federations has its own special struggles to wage against the liquor racket.
I wish to mention particularly the tremendous and dignified work performed by the leagues of the Sacred Heart and the Lacordaire and Joan of Arc organizations in my province. I believe they deserve to be entirely successful and I hope that their work will be fruitful and that the authorities will help them.
As I said a while ago, we need organizations strong enough to face up to anyone.
It is not by sitting back idly that we shall reap success. We therefore urge that every league, every member of such an organization and anyone able to hold a pen write to the Prime Minister and to their member of parliament and support our request: observance of the law.
The Canada Temperance Union has submitted a request published by L'Action Catholique under date of February 11, 1949:
Request to the federal government by the Canada Temperance Union.
In a memorandum submitted yesterday to Prime Minister St. Laurent, the Canada Temperance Union recommends the appointment of a royal commission

to investigate the Canadian liquor problem. A delegation of 12 representatives from religious and temperance organizations met the Prime Minister yesterday afternoon and submitted to him a six-page memorandum.
I understand why certain people would like to restrict the use of alcoholic beverages. Autonomy should not be a factor in my opinion, when we are out to curb mass poisoning, and the unreasoned and unreasonable use of alcoholic beverages.
(Text):
I have an article from the Toronto Star of the 3rd of March, 1949, stating that 30,620 "drunks" were convicted in Ontario in 1948. It reads in part:
Out of the Ontario government's expanding liquor business came 30,620 convictions for drunkenness in 1948 . . .
I do not quote that to sling mud at any province of Canada. I merely do so to arouse public opinion. I want everybody in Canada to know what the situation is and to realize that it is time to rise in force and make the public authorities conscious of the danger confronting our population. That is why I do so. That is why I repeat the same things I said in my first speech on liquor consumption. I want to return to that question, and I hope I shall not be the only one to come back to it, because the time has come when everyone should face his responsibility for the betterment of our Canadian society. I have an editorial from the Ottawa Journal of March 15, 1949, and I note that the danger is present in other provinces. The title of the editorial is:
Still Debauching the Indians
It reads in part:
A disturbing story comes from Alert bay, a small British Columbia settlement 299 miles northwest of Vancouver, with some 600 white residents and a reservation of 1,800 Indians. Greedy and unscrupulous white men are taking liquor into the area by speed-boat and bootlegging it to the Indians at $10 to $25 a bottle, with the result that drunken Indians are a major problem and, according to the Indian superintendent, "it is neither fit nor safe for a woman to walk down Alert bay's one street at night."
As you see, Mr. Speaker, the evil is spreading its tentacles into other parts of our country. I have a calculation made by Mr. Gaudette, the president of the Sacred Heart league. A question was asked in the letter sent to every municipality as to how many quart bottles of milk the amount of liquor consumed in the country in 1947 would provide? The answer was that it would amount to 635,433,900 quarts of milk for the children. I have here a release from the same league and by the same man, Mr. J. Wilfrid Gaudette, president of the Sacred Heart league of the province of

Quebec, on collective temperance, which was distributed by the episcopate of my province. It reads:
(Translation):
Lawgivers, and in them all whose duty it is to approve and enforce the laws, will understand, we are sure, that in the interest of the public it behooves them to practise and respect the virtue of temperance. Need we recall that any person in authority is responsible not only for his own wrongdoing but for leading others astray: he is also accountable for his failure to do good or preventing others from doing good. Finally, he is responsible for all the evil he does not prevent when he can and should do so.
(Text):
The bishops and archbishops of my province have given this warning, and I hope that at last it may be understood and heeded by provincial authorities throughout Canada. I hope we may all face our responsibilities and take steps to see that drinking, which is increasing even among youngsters as well as grown people, is discouraged.
