subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I speak briefly on the budget, may I devote a few minutes to outlining a problem which, though not of national concern, means a great deal to a part of my province.
In the house, I have the privilege and the honour of representing the constituency of Charlevoix. Extending over a distance of 140 miles from Chateau Richer to the Saguenay river, it is largely peopled by French-Canadian catholics. I also wish to state that my constituency is proud of its local history since from there many pioneers set forth to share in the development of certain parts of the lake St. John district and of the north shore.
Because of its topography, my constituency is partly agricultural and partly industrial. Indeed, the lumber industry plays an important part and a growing number of men skilled in that kind of work are to be found in certain municipalities.
This constituency, which borders on the St. Lawrence, is served by a very primitive railway line. The Canadian National has a branch running from Quebec to La Malbaie and, in fact, La Malbaie is actually the terminal of the only railway line in that area. This situation is assuredly unsatisfactory, much more so because its improvements can easily be justified both from an economic point of view and from that of the development of Charlevoix county. As was stated by my friend from the Saguenay and north shore regions, and as is known to the majority of the members of this house, our district is on the threshold of great developments
The Budget-Mr. Maltais which will probably have a tremendous bearing on the economy of this country.
So, I think it is time that, at the request of my fellow citizens, I should bring to the attention of the government the transportation problem as it exists in my constituency. In the near future I intend to ask the proper authorities that improvements be made as regards the line now linking Quebec with La Malbaie. I shall first request that the Canadian National start negotiations with the Quebec Railway, because in my opinion present arrangements between the two are now inadequate and greatly handicap the service we want. I shall then ask that this service be extended from La Malbaie to the municipality of Clermont and that it be made a daily service, since a line is already there and the people of Clermont are entitled to and should obtain such a service. Finally, since the matter of opening a new outlet to the lake St. John and Chicoutimi districts is now being discussed, I shall also request that the line be extended from Clermont to Port Alfred, and that its eventual extension into the county of Saguenay be considered.
This proposal is far more justifiable than that submitted in Quebec city to the royal commission on transportation by the council for the economic development of the Saguenay. I will have the opportunity to prove it at some other time, but meanwhile I wish to quote a thought from Le Feuillet de la semaine, a small local newspaper full of common sense published at Baie St. Paul.
Let it be known, nevertheless, that we refuse to be treated as second-rate citizens, as poor relations. We will never submit to being set aside.
(Text):
It is almost a commonplace to say that the prosperity of this country and the high standard of living enjoyed in our land is closely related to our foreign trade. One who has followed the legislation of this government will soon be convinced that this very important part of our economic life has been dealt with in an effective way. I have learned from many reliable references, and in my short experience in business, that external trade is of paramount importance to the successful development and the welfare of this country. To support this statement I want to quote part of a monthly letter published by the Royal Bank of Canada in June, 1946, which illustrates the importance of external trade to the welfare of Canada. This has reference to the theory of self-sufficiency in Canada, and says:
To dispose in one paragraph of the bogey of what would happen if Canada were so foolish as to adopt a policy of self-sufficiency, contrast the actualities of the past twenty years with what might
1150	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Maltais have been under a nationalistic economy. If Canada had not exported, there would have been an average of $1,365 million a year less entering the flow of money, a reduction of about 27 per cent in the national income, or nearly $10 a month smaller purchasing power for every man, woman and child in the country. If there had not been exports of $8,537 million of farm products in the 19 years preceding 1945, there would have been $614 less income per year per farm.
In other words, Canada just cannot continue on her present standards, much less can she raise them, without foreign markets for her goods.
It is based on the fact that, although Canada is rich in many natural resources, she is lacking in quite a few important commodities. When I refer to an abundance of natural resources, I mean that in certain products, such as wheat, newsprint and different metals, Canada has large surpluses. In many cases a foreign market is necessary in order to liquidate the surpluses. On the other hand, it is no less true to say that we lack certain vital products such as steel, coal, coffee or sugar, as well as certain specialized manufactured goods. This country has to import many items which are necessary to our daily life.
In the last two or three decades this external trade has made great strides, Mr. Speaker. From a value of slightly more than $431 million in 1914, our exports have jumped to approximately $2,750 million in 1947. When one goes over the maze of statistics concerning this period, one is impressed by several features which seem to have a direct bearing on the future of our national economy. I find that up to recent years our exports have been chiefly in the field of primary products, usually referred to as raw material or semi-processed material. Of course, by the very nature of these products they generally react more violently to price cycles than manufactured products.
I refer now to the statistics for the year 1921 which show that Canada received $311 million for 120 million bushels of wheat, whereas in 1939 Canada received approximately $109 million for 163 million bushels. If I pushed my study further I could illustrate this trend with other farm products or

with metals. Helped by the impetus of the last war, however, it is interesting to note that our exports in the last few years have been made up of a larger proportion of manufactured goods. I believe this is a new trend which indicates a greater diversification of our national economy. In view of present world conditions, this certainly affords ground for satisfaction. It is likely this diversification will permit Canada to open new markets. I believe the agreements made at Geneva and at Annecy will also help this country to obtain new markets for the exportation of these new products which Canada seems to be manufacturing in larger quantities.
However, Mr. Speaker, although my remarks might indicate that our foreign trade seems to have become re-oriented, I should like to say at once that we should not neglect our traditional markets, which have always been in the commonwealth. It is well known that the greatest trade exists among the most-developed nations. I believe I am right in saying that this government was very much aware of this principle. When I look at the assistance this government has given Great Britain in the form of mutual aid, I consider it not so much a gift as an investment in the long run economic development of this country.
On motion of Mr. Maltais the debate was adjourned.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow is private members' day, but I understand the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has consulted the leaders of the opposition parties with a view to moving to go into supply, so that he can ask for interim supply. If there is no objection, that will be the first order, and then we will revert to private members' business.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Wednesday, October 26, 1949
